deep.reconstruction: This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations, diagrams or numerical work. It is a fair-copy prose notebook, apparently notes taken from or for a course on ancient Greek history, continuing from the previous page (Marathon, death of Miltiades) into the next (Themistocles' naval programme, Xerxes' invasion of 480 BC). Content of this page: (1) Themistocles made Athens into a naval power, but his character had weak sides. He never took the straight path but a side path, was anything but disinterested, could easily be bribed, and sided now with one party, now with another. Still, the welfare of his fatherland mattered to him above all, as long as it did not conflict with his own advantage. (2) Aristides was a plain, upright man, famous for his virtue and integrity and for his indifference to wealth. His political principles differed entirely from those of Themistocles: Themistocles favoured democracy, Aristides aristocracy. As a general, Themistocles surpassed Aristides. The two men, now at the head of the state, could not be friends. (3) Themistocles was named admiral of the fleet to punish the islands and levy money. He carried this out with great success and enriched Athens, while Aristides stood at the head in Athens. (4) When Themistocles returned, Aristides was banished by ostracism ('Scherbengericht'), dated here 'a. 486'. This left Themistocles alone at the head. (5) He knew Athens had to fear another great war with Persia. The sentence continues on the next page with the fleet-building plan. There is nothing to reconstruct mathematically. The handwriting and the subject matter suggest student lecture notes on history, possibly not in Gauss's hand. Their presence in a bundle labelled 'Lagrange1816' looks like a cataloguing or binding artefact.
errors: No mathematical content, so there are no mathematical errors.
Historical note: the ostracism of Aristides is usually dated to 482 BC, not 486 BC as written ('a. 486'). Some older textbooks gave earlier dates, so this may reflect the source being followed.

The expedition 'to punish the islands' is in the ancient sources (Herodotus 8.111–112) a post-Salamis episode (480/479 BC), not something preceding Aristides' ostracism. The notes conflate it with, or misplace it relative to, Miltiades' earlier island campaign.
